subject: white star
title: What If the Sun Were Twice as Heavy? Earth Would Be Baked

scenes.text: What if the Sun had twice its mass? It wouldn't be twice as bright. Try sixteen times.
Brightness climbs far faster than mass. Double the mass and the glow jumps roughly 16 times. Sirius, at 2 Suns, shines about 25 times brighter.
That light is blue-white, heavy in ultraviolet. Earth, at its current distance, heats to well over 200 degrees Celsius. The oceans boil away.
The comfortable zone moves out to 4 or 5 times Earth's distance, roughly where Jupiter orbits today.
But a heavier star burns its fuel faster. Instead of 10 billion years, this Sun lasts 1 to 2 billion before swelling into a red giant.
On our Earth, life needed almost 4 billion years to make animals. Under a double Sun, the star dies while the oceans are still slime.

description:
What if the Sun were twice as massive? Luminosity rises steeply with mass: a main-sequence star of 2 solar masses shines roughly 16 times brighter than the Sun, and Sirius A, at about 2 solar masses, is about 25 times brighter. Earth at its present orbit would reach an equilibrium temperature well above 200 degrees Celsius, and the habitable zone would move out to around 4 to 5 astronomical units, near Jupiter's orbit.
Heavier stars also burn out faster: a 2-solar-mass star spends only around 1 to 2 billion years on the main sequence, compared with about 10 billion for the Sun. Since complex animal life on Earth took nearly 4 billion years to appear, such a star would die long before it could evolve.

first_comment: Go the other way and a Sun with half its mass would last about 50 billion years but shine so dimly that Earth would need to orbit closer than Mercury. Which star would you rather live under?
